open_points.subject: OwnerFormField, OwnerFormCarrier, and FormValueKind module boundaries
open_points.question: Which logical module owns each of `OwnerFormField`, `OwnerFormCarrier`, and `FormValueKind`, which module publicly exports each type, and—if they are split across modules—which exact direct import edges are required?
options: Own and export all three from `models`, requiring no cross-module edge for the field annotations.
Own `OwnerFormField` in `models` and the two value types in a conventions module; export both value types and import them directly into `models`.
Give each value type a separate provider module and declare the corresponding exports and direct imports.
open_points.default_guess: Own and export all three from `models`.

witness.initial: Generation must create the OwnerFormField model and bind both annotation names.
events: The model generator selects modules for the three types.
A consumer imports OwnerFormField and evaluates or resolves its field annotations.
outcomes: OwnerFormField resolves from `models`, but one or both annotation types are expected from an unstated different provider or are unavailable.
witness.observer: The generator and any consumer importing or reflecting on OwnerFormField.

open_points.subject: Concrete representation of OwnerFormCarrier and FormValueKind
open_points.question: What exact contract representation and member names will encode the already stated carrier categories and value-reading categories?
options: Define both as closed literal unions.
Define validated scalar or tagged-value types with canonical serialized values.
consequences: Enums give named runtime members and require an import wherever members are referenced.
Literal unions reduce runtime machinery but provide no enum-member identity.
Validated tagged values can control serialization explicitly but add construction and validation behavior.
open_points.requirement: A row of the owner form table: one field of the owner's pages — what the owner types or picks in a form — as the owner interface names it on the page and reads it back (owner, 2026-11-25): its name, whether it belongs to the owner's request itself or to the values the owner gives, and how its text is read: as text, as a whole number, as yes or no, or as one of a closed list.
open_points.default_guess: Define both as enums with canonical serialized string values.

set_aside.subject: FormValueKind interpretation rules
set_aside.text: how its text is read: as text, as a whole number, as yes or no, or as one of a closed list.
set_aside.question: For each FormValueKind, what input text is accepted, what normalization is permitted, and what required refusal or error occurs when the text cannot be read as that kind?
options: Define one strict canonical grammar for whole numbers, yes/no, text, and closed-list matching.
Define normalization rules such as trimming, case folding, localized yes/no tokens, and normalized closed-list matching.
Make the release provide the parsing policy for each field.
consequences: A strict grammar is deterministic but may reject common owner input such as alternate case or localized yes/no words.
Normalization is friendlier but requires exact rules to keep modules consistent.
A release-provided policy supports variation but adds release data and a boundary obligation for obtaining it.
set_aside.requirement: how its text is read: as text, as a whole number, as yes or no, or as one of a closed list.
set_aside.default_guess: Trim surrounding whitespace, use a signed base-10 integer grammar, accept case-insensitive canonical yes/no tokens, and require an exact normalized match for closed-list values.

witness.initial: A field has `reads_as` set to yes-or-no and the owner supplies `Yes`; another whole-number field contains ` 12 `.
events: A boundary consumer reads the supplied text using FormValueKind.
The consumer either accepts and converts the text or reports a refusal.
outcomes: The consumer trims and compares case-insensitively, producing true and 12.
The consumer requires canonical unmodified tokens and refuses one or both values.
witness.observer: The owner and any downstream module receiving the converted value or failure.

set_aside.subject: Closed-list choices for OwnerFormField
set_aside.text: as one of a closed list.
set_aside.question: Where is the closed list for a field supplied, how is it associated with that OwnerFormField, and may callers rely on receiving it before reading or validating a value?
options: Add the allowed choices to each applicable field's required facts.
Provide a separate release catalog keyed by stable field identity.
Define a fixed built-in list for every recognized field name.
Treat `reads_as` only as a category and provide no validation list.
consequences: Inline choices make each field self-contained but add required model data.
A separate catalog avoids repetition but requires stable lookup identity and a public lookup obligation.
Built-in lists couple code to field names and require a compatibility rule for release changes.
Without an available list, callers cannot deterministically render or validate the promised closed-list input.
set_aside.requirement: how its text is read: as text, as a whole number, as yes or no, or as one of a closed list.
set_aside.default_guess: Include the allowed choices in the release metadata for each closed-list field.

witness.initial: The release contains a `colour` field whose `reads_as` value denotes a closed list.
events: A consumer obtains the OwnerFormField row.
The consumer must render the owner form and validate the submitted value `blue`.
outcomes: The row or a specified catalog supplies the allowed choices, so rendering and validation are deterministic.
No choices or lookup obligation are specified, so the consumer invents a list or cannot validate the value.
witness.observer: The owner using the form and the module validating the submission.
